title: Cristaux (1970). Gribouillis et calculs divers : notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
The page has two parts: rational slope comparisons on the right and lattice-point drawings on squared paper on the left. All the comparisons are correct. 13/15 < 7/8 since 104 < 105. 3/4 > 11/15 since 45 > 44. 2/3 < 11/16 since 32 < 33. 12/14 = 6/7 is simply a reduction.

The pattern matters more than the inequalities. In each strict comparison the cross-difference is exactly ±1: 7·15 − 8·13 = 1, 3·15 − 4·11 = 1, 2·16 − 3·11 = −1. So the pairs (6/7, 7/8), (13/15, 7/8), (11/15, 3/4) and (2/3, 11/16) are Farey neighbours. Also 13/15 = (6+7)/(7+8) is the mediant of 6/7 and 7/8. The previous page has 4/5 < 13/15 (cross-difference 5, not neighbours) and 14/16 = 7/8.

The drawings plot segments from the origin with rational slopes, endpoints on a vertical line about 15–16 squares to the right, with lattice points marked along them. In the top figure a straight segment of slope about 13/15 (from (1,0) to about (16,13)) is closely shadowed by a broken lattice polygon starting at the origin, whose breakpoints are lattice points next to the segment. The lower figure is a fan of segments of decreasing slope from a common origin, plus one heavier broken polygon approximating the steepest segment from the lattice side.

In modern terms this is Newton-polygon combinatorics for F-crystals and p-divisible groups. A segment from (0,0) to (n,m) with gcd 1 is the Newton polygon of an isoclinic isocrystal of slope m/n. The lattice polygons just above or below it come from breaking at the lattice point nearest the segment. That point is determined by the Farey neighbours of m/n: the triangle has no interior lattice point, by Pick's theorem, exactly when the determinant is ±1. So one gets polygons with slopes 6/7 and 7/8 adjacent to slope 13/15.

This is the combinatorics behind the specialization of Newton polygons. Grothendieck's theorem says the Newton polygon rises under specialization. He conjectured the converse at Montréal in 1970, and Oort later proved it, with codimension counted by lattice points. The page is consistent with Grothendieck's work on Barsotti–Tate groups and Dieudonné crystals (1970). The next page continues with the Tannakian category of filtered F-crystals and Hodge versus Newton data. The page is scratch work: enumerating adjacent slopes and minimal Newton polygons, with no stated result.
errors: No arithmetic errors; all comparisons check. The interpretation of the drawings (exact slopes and endpoints) is uncertain from the image.

ideas.what: Testing adjacency of rational slopes via cross-difference ±1 (Farey neighbours, mediant 13/15 of 6/7 and 7/8)
ideas.modern_name: Farey neighbours / Stern–Brocot adjacency; empty lattice triangles (Pick)

ideas.what: Lattice polygons approximating a straight segment of rational slope: Newton polygons immediately adjacent to an isoclinic one
ideas.modern_name: Newton polygon strata; specialization of Newton polygons and its converse (Grothendieck conjecture)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Grothendieck (specialization theorem, conjecture 1970); Katz (1979); Oort (2000-2001, converse and purity); de Jong–Oort
ideas.where_published: Groupes de Barsotti-Tate et cristaux de Dieudonné (Montréal 1970, publ. 1974); letter to Barsotti 1970

deep.surprise_reason: Scratch combinatorics of rational slopes and lattice polygons, consistent with Grothendieck's known 1970 work on Newton-polygon specialization of F-crystals and Barsotti–Tate groups. It is a nice glimpse of him checking Farey adjacency, but contains nothing beyond the known theory.
transcription_corrections: Transcription omits the two figures: the top one is a segment of slope ~13/15 shadowed by a broken lattice polygon from the origin; the bottom one is a fan of segments from a common origin with lattice points marked, plus a heavier broken polygon.
The faint marks below '2/3 < 11/16' look like a further fraction comparison (perhaps with a 'not equal' sign), illegible.
'59' at the bottom left is the archive page number, not mathematics.
